title: Nginx and HTTPS
summary: Keep the Boot listener local, forward trusted public request details, and serve HTTPS through Nginx.

sources.title: Spring Boot: traditional deployment and proxy configuration

richText: Boot behind the HTTPS proxy
Nginx can forward public requests to the Boot process from the preceding VPS lesson.
Boot’s
server.address=127.0.0.1
c
keeps its HTTP listener local to that VPS.
Nginx accepts public HTTPS and forwards to
c
The application sees the proxy connection unless the server uses trusted forwarded headers. This matters for generated redirects and external callback URLs.
Forwarded headers in Boot
server.forward-headers-strategy=NATIVE
c
enables the embedded server’s forwarded-header handling.
With Tomcat, this uses its remote-IP support. The trusted proxy configuration must match the actual proxy network.
Forwarded headers are trusted input only when an approved proxy sets them and direct public access to the application is blocked.
In this single-proxy arrangement, Nginx replaces forwarded values with the public request information.
Nginx and application configuration

example.title: Forward HTTPS to the local Boot server
description: Java `17` and Maven are required. The files form a separate project rooted at `pom.xml`.
The Linux host uses systemd and Java `17` at `/usr/bin/java`. The `demo` account and group already exist.
The commands run on the host from the project root. `/opt/demo` already exists. The service account can read its JAR but cannot replace it.
The root-owned `/etc/demo.env` file has restricted permissions. The two absolute-path tabs show host configuration files.
`demo.example.com` represents a domain controlled by the application owner. Its DNS points to the VPS.
A valid certificate and matching private key for that domain already exist at the displayed paths.
The Nginx process can read the required certificate files. Private-key permissions restrict other access.
The application restarts after those environment changes. Network rules allow public HTTPS but keep port `8080` private.
This example uses TLS `1.3`. The installed Nginx and its TLS library must support it.
Each host configuration tab is saved at its displayed absolute path before the service commands run.
explanation: The HTTP block redirects to the fixed HTTPS domain.
Nginx supplies the public scheme, port, fixed host, and client address. It discards a caller-supplied `Forwarded` header.
The Actuator prefix is blocked on this public route. Local monitoring can still use its separately controlled access path.
`nginx -t` checks the configuration and readable certificate files before the reload command runs.
The final request checks TLS and the public proxy route. Its status depends on the application mappings and access rules.
example.commands:
mvn clean package
sudo install -o root -g demo -m 640 target/demo.jar /opt/demo/demo.jar
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now demo.service
sudo systemctl restart demo.service
systemctl status demo.service
journalctl -u demo.service -n 100 --no-pager
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/
sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx
curl -i https://demo.example.com/

files.code:
# /etc/systemd/system/demo.service
[Unit]
Description=Demo application
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=demo
Group=demo
WorkingDirectory=/opt/demo
EnvironmentFile=/etc/demo.env
ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -jar /opt/demo/demo.jar
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
TimeoutStopSec=60
NoNewPrivileges=true

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

richText: Certificates and connection behavior
The served certificate must match the public domain and remain valid. Certificate renewal must also reload the renewed certificate into Nginx.
Request-size limits and proxy timeouts must match the application’s supported requests.
A local Boot response, a public HTTPS response, and an authenticated database operation check different parts of the release.
An HTTPS response alone does not prove that the application can reach its database or apply its access rules.
